messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Figures: People in uniform, Military Topics: Talks about military, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Carry Weapon: carry weapon, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ernesto Villanueva is a 70-year-old widowed dentist of Colombian origin who has practiced in the same Miami clinic for nearly three decades. He came to the United States as a young man, built a quiet, ordered life, and prided himself on a steadiness that his patients and colleagues had always remarked upon. That steadiness was fractured approximately fourteen months ago when Ernesto was present at a civic ceremony in a public park — a local festival he attended every year — when a politically motivated attack unfolded without warning. Armed men in paramilitary-style clothing moved through the crowd, firing weapons and shouting directives. Ernesto was pinned behind a vendor's cart for what felt to him like an eternity, pressed against the ground, listening to shots ring out at irregular intervals, watching uniformed figures move past him with weapons raised. He was not physically wounded, but a man standing near him was struck and fell. Ernesto did not run. He stayed still, and he has never fully made peace with that fact.

In the weeks after the attack, Ernesto returned to his practice because he did not know what else to do. The clinic's routine — the hum of the suction unit, the bright overhead lights, the predictable sequencing of appointments — offered something that resembled normalcy. But the world outside the operatory had become a different place. When a car backfired on the street near his clinic, Ernesto found himself gripping the edge of the sink, unable to move for several seconds, the park flooding back through him not as a recollection but as a full sensory return: the smell of the grass, the weight of the ground beneath him, the sound of the shots as immediate and present as if they were occurring in the room. When the memory came in those moments, it did not arrive as narrative — he could not have told anyone, in ordered sentences, what had happened or in what sequence. It came as sensation, as texture, as the particular quality of light that afternoon, and it overwhelmed him so completely that he sometimes had to excuse himself from a patient mid-procedure and stand in the back hallway until the wave passed.

Ernesto had come to believe, with a certainty that felt irrefutable to him, that he should have done something more — pulled the man beside him to safety, acted rather than frozen. He returned to this conclusion repeatedly, rehearsing the moment from every angle, always arriving at the same verdict against himself. He began avoiding the evening news, because any report touching on political violence or armed groups confirmed, in his mind, that the world remained exactly as dangerous as it had been that afternoon. He started carrying a licensed firearm, which he kept in his car and sometimes in the inner pocket of his jacket, because what frightened him most was the idea of being caught without any means of response again.

At the clinic, the consequences of these changes became visible in ways Ernesto could not fully conceal. When a patient arrived wearing a security guard's uniform for an afternoon appointment, Ernesto felt his chest tighten and his attention fracture entirely. He got through the appointment by watching the man's hands. He now scans the waiting room each morning before unlocking the front door — not consciously cataloguing exits, but moving his eyes to every corner and doorway in a sweep that has become as automatic as washing his hands. He monitors his patients and his staff with a vigilance that has no clinical purpose, reading faces for signs of something he cannot name precisely but recognises immediately as threat.

A colleague gently noted that Ernesto seemed changed, and that several patients had mentioned he seemed distracted. A conversation about a recent news story involving military operations in South America left Ernesto unable to concentrate for the remainder of the afternoon. It was his daughter, calling from Bogotá, who finally said what had been unsaid — that her father did not sound like himself, and had not for over a year. Ernesto made the appointment the following week. What he most hopes for is to be able to remember what happened without being destroyed by it each time. What he fears most is that the man he was before the park no longer exists.
